claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy has enhanced mechanical performance relative to its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The quinary alloy has a greater degree of local chemical short-range order than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater local chemical short-range order induces heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Heterogeneous lattice distortions locally impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion produces more effective strain hardening during deformation.
All compared alloys are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing ensures comparable grain size, phase distribution, and defect density across the alloys.
Increased configurational complexity in the quinary alloy promotes local variations in bonding and atomic spacing.
Local variations in bonding and atomic spacing create variable energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Variable energy barriers cause stronger dislocation pinning and higher strain hardening in the quinary alloy.
Reduced compositional complexity in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces a more uniform lattice with fewer energetic obstacles to dislocation motion.
The quinary alloy will exhibit higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary subsets under the stated test conditions.
The quinary alloy will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary subsets under the stated test conditions.
In situ deformation measurements will show increased dislocation interactions in the quinary alloy.
In situ measurements will show SRO evolution in the quinary alloy that correlates with its enhanced mechanical response.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the compared alloys remain single-phase FCC and are deformed at identical temperature and strain rate.
Direct quantitative correlations between SRO and mechanical properties have not been firmly established in these specific alloy systems.
